reference.source: Smith's Recognizable Patterns of Human Malformation / GeneReviews
clinicalPearls: One of the acromelic dysplasias: severe short stature with strikingly short hands and feet and progressive joint stiffness/contractures
The characteristic 'happy' or pleasant round facial appearance gives the condition its name (from the Greek for happy face)
Progressive cardiac valve disease and airway/tracheal narrowing are the main life-threatening complications
Caused by variants in ADAMTSL2 (autosomal recessive) or in a specific region of FBN1 (autosomal dominant), converging on abnormal TGF-beta signalling and microfibril handling
Thickened skin, hepatomegaly and recurrent respiratory infections are frequent
Radiographs show short tubular bones, cone-shaped epiphyses and a characteristic pattern in the hands
Management is supportive with close cardiac and respiratory surveillance; valve and airway disease drive morbidity and mortality
reference.pathophysiology: Geleophysic dysplasia arises from disturbance of the extracellular microfibril-transforming growth factor beta (TGF-beta) system. Recessive variants in ADAMTSL2, a secreted protein that interacts with fibrillin microfibrils, and dominant variants in a particular domain of FBN1 both dysregulate TGF-beta bioavailability and signalling within connective tissue. The resulting abnormal matrix produces the acromelic (distal-limb) shortening, joint contractures, thickened skin, and, importantly, progressive infiltration and fibrosis of cardiac valves and the airway that determine prognosis.
additionalDifferentials: Other acromelic dysplasias with short hands
additionalInvestigations: Targeted analysis of ADAMTSL2 and FBN1, ideally via a skeletal dysplasia gene panel
Skeletal survey demonstrating short tubular bones and cone-shaped epiphyses
Echocardiography to assess for progressive valvular disease
Airway and respiratory assessment including imaging for tracheal narrowing
redFlags: Progressive valvular heart disease with signs of cardiac failure
Airway compromise or stridor from tracheal or laryngeal narrowing
Rapidly worsening joint contractures limiting function
reference.prognosis: Prognosis is guarded because progressive cardiac valve disease and airway narrowing frequently cause serious morbidity and can lead to early death, particularly in severe forms, although milder cases survive into adulthood with supportive care.
pitfalls: Mistaking the storage-like facies and hepatomegaly for a mucopolysaccharidosis
Underestimating progressive cardiac valve involvement that may worsen over time
Overlooking silent airway narrowing until acute respiratory compromise occurs
Failing to distinguish it from the milder, cardiologically less involved acromicric dysplasia
references: Smith's Recognizable Patterns of Human Malformation
management: No disease-specific drug therapy exists, so care is supportive and directed at the life-threatening cardiorespiratory complications
Serial echocardiographic surveillance for progressive valvular thickening, with valve repair or replacement when haemodynamically significant
Airway assessment and management of tracheal and laryngeal narrowing, which may require tracheostomy and long-term respiratory support
Prompt treatment and prevention of the frequent respiratory infections
Orthopaedic and physiotherapy management of joint contractures and short-limbed stature
Cautious anaesthetic planning given the difficult airway and cardiac risk, with abdominal monitoring for hepatomegaly
Genetic counselling reflecting autosomal recessive ADAMTSL2 and autosomal dominant FBN1 forms, with coordinated multidisciplinary follow-up
